articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian 'Shadow Banking' Network in Latest Action
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 23, 2026. This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeted over two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel. The aim is to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks, which are described as the regime's 'last financial lifeline' amidst declining oil revenues and economic sanctions.

The designated entities and individuals are accused of facilitating billions of dollars in transactions through the international financial system, providing the Iranian regime with access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions. The action was taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, E.O. 13224, as amended, a counter-terrorism designation authority, and E.O. 13871, which targets persons operating in various sectors of Iran's metals industry.

This move follows previous actions under 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which commenced on August 24, 2026, and aims to sever the remaining economic lifelines sustaining the Iranian regime. Financial institutions are cautioned about potential sanctions exposure for engaging in transactions with these newly designated or otherwise blocked persons.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Iranian Oil Facilitators and Issues New Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced Iran-related designations and the issuance of Cuba Frequently Asked Questions on November 20, 2026. This action targeted four individuals identified as being involved in facilitating Iranian oil sales and recovering oil proceeds held in third countries.

These designations were imposed pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, and E.O. 13224, as amended, the United States' counterterrorism sanctions authority. The move is part of a broader effort to disrupt networks that provide revenue to the Iranian regime.

In addition to the Iran designations, OFAC also issued new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba sanctions. While the specific content of the FAQs was not detailed in the announcement, they aim to provide guidance on existing Cuba sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Narcotics and Cyber Networks, Amends Russia-Related General License
body: On November 19, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting counter narcotics and cyber-related activities. Concurrently, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License and an amended Russia-related General License along with new Frequently Asked Questions.

The counter narcotics designations targeted 14 individuals and six entities tied to international narcotics trafficking, including the Italian 'Ndrangheta and the Comanchero Outlaw Motorcycle Gang, under Executive Order 14059. These actions aim to disrupt transnational criminal networks involved in illicit drug trade.

The amended Russia-related General License and associated FAQs indicate ongoing adjustments to sanctions against Russia. While specific details of the amendments were not immediately available, such changes typically aim to clarify permissible activities or address evolving circumstances in the sanctions landscape.

body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism Designations on November 18, 2026. These designations are part of the ongoing efforts by the U.S. government to combat global terrorism and disrupt financial support networks for terrorist organizations.

While specific entities and individuals were not detailed in the initial announcement, such designations typically involve freezing assets and prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated parties. These actions are taken under existing counter-terrorism authorities, such as Executive Order 13224, as amended.

These designations underscore the U.S. commitment to using financial tools to counter terrorism and protect national security interests by targeting those who provide material support to terrorist activities.

The U.S. government continues to leverage its sanctions authorities to combat a range of illicit activities that pose a threat to international security and stability.

The U.S. Department of State highlighted these sanctions as part of a broader strategy to cripple financial networks sustaining the Iranian regime. These designations aim to further isolate Iran from the international financial system and limit its ability to fund illicit activities.
Such designations typically involve freezing assets under U.S. jurisdiction and prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated individuals and entities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related activities and transnational criminal organizations. Additionally, OFAC imposed new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination.

The Cuba designations targeted a crude oil shipping network, state-owned entities, and China-based suppliers of Cuba's military forces. This action was accompanied by a determination paving the way for further sanctions on the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the U.S. would not tolerate the Cuban regime funneling resources to its military elite or serving as a staging ground for hostile anti-American actors. This marks an escalation in the Trump administration's economic pressure campaign against Cuba, with Chinese companies being targeted for the first time.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Iran-Related Entities, Amends Venezuela-Related General License
body: On November 4, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, updates to certain Iran-related listings, and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert. Concurrently, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a Frequently Asked Question.

The Iran-related actions are part of ongoing efforts to target fraudulent ship registries and aviation support for the Iranian regime. These measures aim to disrupt Iran's ability to circumvent sanctions and fund its illicit activities.

The amended Venezuela-related General License and FAQ indicate adjustments to the U.S. sanctions policy towards Venezuela. While sanctions on Venezuela remain in force, they have been eased through licenses allowing, with conditions, trading oil, gold, and minerals, and using Venezuelan banks. This particular amendment likely extends legal protections shielding bond transactions involving Venezuelan state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela, S.A. (PDVSA) until November 5, 2026.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
